claim: The influenza A virus (IAV) genome consists of eight negative-sense viral RNA (vRNA) segments.
source: The influenza A virus (IAV) genome consists of eight negative-sense viral RNA (vRNA) segments that are selectively assembled into progeny virus particles through RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about IAV genome structure stated in the abstract.

claim: IAV vRNA segments are selectively assembled into progeny virus particles through RNA-RNA interactions.
source: The influenza A virus (IAV) genome consists of eight negative-sense viral RNA (vRNA) segments that are selectively assembled into progeny virus particles through RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Intersegmental tree similarity differed between subtype and lineage.
source: Intersegmental tree similarity differed between subtype and lineage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2-5.

claim: Intersegmental relationships were largely conserved over time in H3N2 viruses.
source: While intersegmental relationships were largely conserved over time in H3N2 viruses, they diverged in H1N1 strains isolated before and after the 2009 pandemic.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Intersegmental relationships diverged in H1N1 strains isolated before and after the 2009 pandemic.
source: While intersegmental relationships were largely conserved over time in H3N2 viruses, they diverged in H1N1 strains isolated before and after the 2009 pandemic.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Intersegmental relationships were not driven solely by protein sequence.
source: Surprisingly, intersegmental relationships were not driven solely by protein sequence, suggesting that IAV evolution could also be driven by RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 comparing gene and protein tree distances.

claim: IAV evolution could be driven by RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Surprisingly, intersegmental relationships were not driven solely by protein sequence, suggesting that IAV evolution could also be driven by RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is presented as an inference from the finding that gene tree similarity is not solely explained by protein tree similarity.

claim: Colocalization of highly coevolved vRNA segments is enriched over other assembly intermediates at the nuclear periphery during productive viral infection.
source: Finally, we used confocal microscopy to determine that colocalization of highly coevolved vRNA segments is enriched over other assembly intermediates at the nuclear periphery during productive viral infection.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by microscopy data in Figure 7.

claim: Rapid evolution of RNA viruses can occur as a result of mutation, recombination, or reassortment.
source: The rapid evolution underlying this variation can occur as a result of mutation, recombination, or reassortment, with major consequences for human disease (Andino and Domingo, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Influenza A virus pandemics occurred in 1918 (H1N1), 1957 (H2N2), 1968 (H3N2), and 2009 (H1N1).
source: Within the past century, influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics occurred in 1918 (H1N1), 1957 (H2N2), 1968 (H3N2), and 2009 (H1N1) (Neumann et al., 2009; Paules and Subbarao, 2017; Short et al., 2018).
evidence: This is historical fact supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each of the last three influenza pandemics was attributable to a reassortant strain composed of a novel combination of the eight vRNA segments.
source: Each of the last three influenza pandemics was attributable to a reassortant strain composed of a novel combination of the eight viral RNA (vRNA) segments of the influenza virus genome (Neumann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Reassortment of vRNA segments must occur during selective assembly of all eight genomic segments, which occurs after export of vRNA segments from the nucleus.
source: Reassortment of vRNA segments must occur during selective assembly of all eight genomic segments, which occurs after export of vRNA segments from the nucleus (Lakdawala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Selective assembly is thought to be facilitated by intersegmental RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Selective assembly is thought to be facilitated by intersegmental RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a current understanding in the field.

claim: Each vRNA segment encodes packaging signals that must be compatible for reassortment to occur.
source: Each vRNA segment encodes packaging signals that must be compatible for reassortment to occur (Lowen, 2017; Richard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Disruption of interactions between two vRNA segments can alter interactions with other segments.
source: Although much remains unknown about the role of RNA-RNA interactions in genomic assembly, it is evident that disruption of interactions between two vRNA segments can alter interactions with other segments, leading to a model in which hierarchical interactions between vRNA segments ensure selective assembly (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020; Marsh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Hierarchical interactions between vRNA segments ensure selective assembly.
source: Although much remains unknown about the role of RNA-RNA interactions in genomic assembly, it is evident that disruption of interactions between two vRNA segments can alter interactions with other segments, leading to a model in which hierarchical interactions between vRNA segments ensure selective assembly (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020; Marsh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a model supported by citations.

claim: The Robinson-Foulds distance (RF) is a widely used measure of topological distance between trees.
source: To evaluate phylogenetic relationships among vRNA segments, we relied upon the Robinson-Foulds distance (RF), a widely used measure of topological distance between trees (Robinson and Foulds, 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The Robinson-Foulds distance determines the number of branch partitions that are not shared between two trees.
source: This method determines the number of branch partitions that are not shared between two trees (Robinson and Foulds, 1981) and is therefore a quantitative measure of the topological distance between trees.
evidence: This is a description of the RF method with a supporting citation.

claim: Lower RF/CID corresponds with greater tree similarity, with a tree distance of 0 indicating that two trees are topologically equivalent.
source: Lower RF/CID corresponds with greater tree similarity, with a tree distance of 0 indicating that two trees are topologically equivalent.
evidence: This is a description of how the distance metrics are interpreted.

claim: Incompatible polymerase subunits exhibit replication deficiencies and are known restriction factors in reassortment.
source: Incompatible polymerase subunits exhibit replication deficiencies and are known restriction factors in reassortment (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Trees built from PB2, PB1, and PA would have high similarity, reflective of a shared evolutionary trajectory.
source: Accordingly, we would predict that trees built from PB2, PB1, and PA would have high similarity, reflective of a shared evolutionary trajectory.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on known protein interactions.

claim: Direct intermolecular interactions between vRNA segments coordinate selective assembly.
source: Likewise, mounting evidence from our group and others suggests that direct intermolecular interactions between vRNA segments coordinate selective assembly (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as mounting evidence with supporting citations.

claim: Genomic assembly occurs in the cytoplasm after nuclear export.
source: Since genomic assembly occurs in the cytoplasm after nuclear export (Lakdawala et al., 2014), we reasoned that assembly intermediates found in close proximity to the nucleus could serve as scaffolds for genomic assembly and sought to visualize this by confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have cocirculated in the human population since 1977.
source: H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have cocirculated in the human population since 1977 (Neumann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with a supporting citation.

claim: 1026 H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004 were available in the Influenza Research Database.
source: We began our investigation with all seasonal human H3N2 viruses for which full-length sequence information was available in the Influenza Research Database (IRD), yielding 1026 H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004 and 3879 H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 1.

claim: 3879 H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014 were available in the Influenza Research Database.
source: We began our investigation with all seasonal human H3N2 viruses for which full-length sequence information was available in the Influenza Research Database (IRD), yielding 1026 H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004 and 3879 H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 1.

claim: A preliminary analysis of 300 sequences suggested that a great deal of phylogenetic variation could not be statistically supported by bootstrapping (branch support less than 70).
source: Reconstructing phylogenetic trees from all available sequences was disadvantageous, as a preliminary analysis of 300 sequences suggested that a great deal of phylogenetic variation could not be statistically supported by bootstrapping (branch support less than 70).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from preliminary analysis.

claim: Trees built from the PB1 and PA segments had low tree distances (RF = 6 and CID = 0.25) in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014.
source: Trees built from the PB1 and PA segments had low tree distances (RF = 6 and CID = 0.25) (Figure 2A), suggesting that these genes evolve in parallel.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PB1 and PA genes evolve in parallel.
source: Trees built from the PB1 and PA segments had low tree distances (RF = 6 and CID = 0.25) (Figure 2A), suggesting that these genes evolve in parallel.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the low tree distance data.

claim: PB1 and HA trees from H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014 had higher tree distances (RF = 14 and CID = 0.44).
source: PB1 and HA trees from the same set of H3N2 strains had higher tree distances (RF = 14 and CID = 0.44) (Figure 2B), suggesting that parallel evolution between PB1 and HA is weaker than that of PB1 and PA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Parallel evolution between PB1 and HA is weaker than that of PB1 and PA.
source: PB1 and HA trees from the same set of H3N2 strains had higher tree distances (RF = 14 and CID = 0.44) (Figure 2B), suggesting that parallel evolution between PB1 and HA is weaker than that of PB1 and PA.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the tree distance comparison.

claim: Tree similarity can be used to identify direct intermolecular interactions that constrain evolution, leading to converging evolutionary trajectories in the trees.
source: These data are consistent with known protein interactions between PB1 and PA and suggest that tree similarity can be used to identify direct intermolecular interactions that constrain evolution, leading to converging evolutionary trajectories in the trees.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the PB1-PA tree similarity data.

claim: The mean RF of vRNA trees from H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014 ranged from 6.5 (PB1 and PA) to 15 (PA and NS).
source: By comparison, the mean RF of vRNA trees ranged from 6.5 (PB1 and PA) to 15 (PA and NS).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The PB2 tree shared the highest similarity with the NA tree rather than the PB1 or PA trees in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014.
source: Surprisingly, the PB2 tree shared the highest similarity with the NA tree rather than the PB1 or PA trees, suggesting that the relationship between PB2 and NA may supercede the essential role of the PB2 protein in the polymerase complex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The relationship between PB2 and NA may supercede the essential role of the PB2 protein in the polymerase complex.
source: Surprisingly, the PB2 tree shared the highest similarity with the NA tree rather than the PB1 or PA trees, suggesting that the relationship between PB2 and NA may supercede the essential role of the PB2 protein in the polymerase complex.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the tree similarity data.

claim: Pairwise intersegmental relationships determined by RF were remarkably reproducible when compared to CID.
source: Pairwise intersegmental relationships determined by RF were remarkably reproducible when compared to CID (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is robust parallel evolution between PB1, PA, NP, and NA in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014.
source: These networks reveal robust parallel evolution between PB1, PA, NP, and NA in H3N2 viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the network analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tree distances ranged widely in H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004, with the highest tree similarity found between PB1, PA, NP, and NA trees.
source: As was seen in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014, tree distances ranged widely, with the highest tree similarity found between PB1, PA, NP, and NA trees of this time period.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Statistical differences between RF from each time period were only found for the NS segment in H3N2 viruses.
source: Statistical differences between RF from each time period were only found for the NS segment (Figure 3C; refer to Supplementary file 6 for exact p-values).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Tree distances for H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004 were positively correlated with those from 2005 to 2014.
source: Finally, tree distances for H3N2 viruses from 1995 to 2004 were positively correlated with those from 2005 to 2014 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Phylogenetic relationships between vRNA segments in H3N2 viruses are largely conserved across the two time periods (1995-2004 and 2005-2014).
source: Taken together, we conclude that phylogenetic relationships between vRNA segments in H3N2 viruses are largely conserved across these two time periods.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data in Figure 3.

claim: The 2009 pandemic was caused by an antigenically shifted H1N1 virus that emerged from reassortment of two swine-origin viruses.
source: This pandemic was caused by an antigenically shifted H1N1 virus that emerged from reassortment of two swine-origin viruses, the North American triple reassortant swine H1N1 virus and Eurasian swine H1N1 virus (Garten et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with a supporting citation.

claim: Tree distances from H1N1 viruses shared either a modest negative correlation or none at all with H3N2 viruses from either time period.
source: Using linear regression, we found that tree distances from H1N1 viruses shared either a modest negative correlation or none at all with H3N2 viruses from either time period (Figure 4B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the referenced figures.

claim: Parallel evolution between vRNA segments overall have significantly diverged between seasonal human influenza H1N1 and H3N2 viruses from similar time scales.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that parallel evolution between vRNA segments overall have significantly diverged between seasonal human influenza H1N1 and H3N2 viruses from similar time scales.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison of tree distances between H1N1 and H3N2 viruses.

claim: Many relationships between vRNA segments were disrupted in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses compared to pre-pandemic H1N1 viruses.
source: In stark contrast to the relatively conserved vRNA relationships observed in H3N2 viruses over time, many relationships between vRNA segments were disrupted in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Parallel evolution between PB1 and NP observed in pre-pandemic H1N1 viruses (mean RF increased from 1 to 5) was notably displaced by stronger coevolution of PB1 with NA in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses (mean RF decreased from 9 to 3).
source: Parallel evolution between PB1 and NP observed in pre-pandemic H1N1 viruses (mean RF increased from 1 to 5) was notably displaced by stronger coevolution of PB1 with NA in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses (mean RF decreased from 9 to 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The M and NS trees shared similar topologies across H1N1 lineages, but each one was significantly more coevolved with the HA and NA trees in post-pandemic viruses.
source: The M and NS trees shared similar topologies across H1N1 lineages, but each one was significantly more coevolved with the HA and NA trees in post-pandemic viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The PB2 trees diverged significantly from the PA trees in favor of greater parallel evolution with the NP and NS trees in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses.
source: The PB2 trees diverged significantly from the PA trees in favor of greater parallel evolution with the NP and NS trees in post-pandemic H1N1 viruses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Shared evolutionary trajectories have significantly diverged between H1N1 lineages.
source: However, these data imply that shared evolutionary trajectories have significantly diverged between H1N1 lineages.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data comparing pre- and post-pandemic H1N1 viruses.

claim: The genomic segments of the swine-origin 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus were contributed by human, avian, and swine hosts.
source: The genomic segments of the swine-origin 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus were contributed by human, avian, and swine hosts (Garten et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Host origin may impact the evolutionary trajectory of emerging reassortant viruses from different lineages and the resultant relationships between genomic segments of contemporary H1N1 viruses in humans.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that host origin may impact the evolutionary trajectory of emerging reassortant viruses from different lineages and the resultant relationships between genomic segments of contemporary H1N1 viruses in humans.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that H1N1 lineages with different host origins have different vRNA relationships.

claim: Known protein relationships between PB1 and PA, two members of the polymerase complex, are captured by the phylogenetic tree similarity approach.
source: We have already shown that known protein relationships between PB1 and PA, two members of the polymerase complex, are captured by our approach (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: PB2 is more coevolved with NA than with either PB1 or PA in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014.
source: However, the observation that PB2, another member of the polymerase complex, is more coevolved with NA than with either PB1 or PA (Figure 2C) suggests that our method also reveals protein-independent parallel evolution, since these proteins are not known to function together during infection.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The phylogenetic tree similarity method reveals protein-independent parallel evolution.
source: However, the observation that PB2, another member of the polymerase complex, is more coevolved with NA than with either PB1 or PA (Figure 2C) suggests that our method also reveals protein-independent parallel evolution, since these proteins are not known to function together during infection.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the PB2-NA tree similarity data.

claim: The greatest degree of parallel evolution in protein trees was between HA and NA in H3N2 viruses from 2005 to 2014.
source: As might be expected, the greatest degree of parallel evolution lying at the core of this network was between HA and NA, two viral glycoproteins with coordinated functions in attachment, motility, and entry (Bloom et al., 2010; Sakai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HA and NA are two viral glycoproteins with coordinated functions in attachment, motility, and entry.
source: As might be expected, the greatest degree of parallel evolution lying at the core of this network was between HA and NA, two viral glycoproteins with coordinated functions in attachment, motility, and entry (Bloom et al., 2010; Sakai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: HA and NA were the only pair of vRNA segments that lay significantly above the identity line when comparing gene and protein tree distances.
source: Interestingly, HA and NA were the only pair of vRNA segments that lay significantly above the identity line, strongly supporting the observation made by others that epistatic interactions between these proteins constrain their evolution (Jang and Bae, 2018; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2011; Neverov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6.

claim: Epistatic interactions between HA and NA proteins constrain their evolution.
source: Interestingly, HA and NA were the only pair of vRNA segments that lay significantly above the identity line, strongly supporting the observation made by others that epistatic interactions between these proteins constrain their evolution (Jang and Bae, 2018; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2011; Neverov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Several vRNA segments, such as PB2 and NA, lay significantly below the identity line when comparing gene and protein tree distances.
source: Of particular interest was that several vRNA segments, such as PB2 and NA (Figure 6, open diamond), lay significantly below the identity line.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6.

claim: vRNA segments lying below the identity line could be indicative of either purifying selection or of greater parallel evolution between the vRNA segments than the proteins encoded.
source: This could be indicative of either purifying selection or of greater parallel evolution between the vRNA segments than the proteins encoded.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 6.

claim: Parallel evolution may identify putative RNA interactions between vRNA segments that could facilitate selective assembly and packaging.
source: These observations suggest that parallel evolution may identify putative RNA interactions between vRNA segments that could facilitate selective assembly and packaging.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that some vRNA pairs show greater gene tree similarity than protein tree similarity.

claim: During influenza virus infection, vRNA are synthesized in the nucleus, bound by NP in vRNP complexes, and then transported to the plasma membrane for packaging on endocytic vesicles.
source: During influenza virus infection, vRNA are synthesized in the nucleus, bound by NP in viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) complexes, and then transported to the plasma membrane for packaging on endocytic vesicles (Lakdawala et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Direct RNA-RNA interactions are thought to drive selective assembly of all eight vRNA segments into virus particles, with a hierarchy existing between interactions.
source: Direct RNA-RNA interactions are thought to drive selective assembly of all eight vRNA segments into virus particles, with a hierarchy existing between interactions (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020; Le Sage et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: After genomic replication, vRNA segments are exported from the nucleus as incomplete subcomplexes, or assembly intermediates.
source: Previous studies examining the intracellular localization of vRNA segments demonstrated that after genomic replication, vRNA segments are exported from the nucleus as incomplete subcomplexes, or assembly intermediates (Lakdawala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The formation of complete complexes containing all eight segments occurs en route to the plasma membrane through dynamic fusion or fission of vRNA segments.
source: The formation of complete complexes containing all eight segments occurs en route to the plasma membrane through dynamic fusion or fission of vRNA segments (Bhagwat et al., 2020; Lakdawala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Interactions between some vRNA segments may serve as a scaffold that facilitates formation of complete complexes of all eight vRNA segments.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that interactions between some vRNA segments may serve as a scaffold that facilitates formation of complete complexes of all eight vRNA segments.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the cited studies on vRNA assembly.

claim: The majority of cytoplasmic foci contained all three vRNA segments (PB2, NA, and NS) in H3N2 virus-infected cells.
source: Whole cytoplasmic analysis of vRNP colocalization in 15 individually analyzed cells revealed that the majority of cytoplasmic foci contained all three vRNA segments (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7C.

claim: PB2-NA vRNP complexes are enriched over either NA-NS or PB2-NS vRNP complexes within 300 nm of the nuclear periphery.
source: Examination of newly exported vRNP complexes within 300 nm of the nuclear periphery revealed an enrichment of PB2-NA vRNP complexes over either NA-NS or PB2-NS vRNP complexes (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7D.

claim: PB2 and NA preferentially colocalize with each other after nuclear synthesis.
source: These data indicate that PB2 and NA preferentially colocalize with each other after nuclear synthesis and support the hypothesis that parallel evolution between segments can reveal putative RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the microscopy data in Figure 7D.

claim: Parallel evolution between segments can reveal putative RNA-RNA interactions.
source: These data indicate that PB2 and NA preferentially colocalize with each other after nuclear synthesis and support the hypothesis that parallel evolution between segments can reveal putative RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by the PB2-NA colocalization data.

claim: RNA-RNA interactions, in addition to protein interactions, are novel drivers of parallel evolution between vRNA segments in seasonal human influenza viruses.
source: Moreover, these data implicate RNA-RNA interactions, in addition to protein interactions, as novel drivers of parallel evolution between vRNA segments in seasonal human influenza viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined phylogenetic and microscopy data.

claim: Parallel evolution varies considerably between vRNA segments, with distinct relationships forming in different influenza virus subtypes (H1N1 vs. H3N2) and between H1N1 virus lineages arising from distinct evolutionary paths.
source: We found that parallel evolution varies considerably between vRNA segments, with distinct relationships forming in different influenza virus subtypes (H1N1 vs. H3N2) and between H1N1 virus lineages arising from distinct evolutionary paths.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Evolutionary relatedness between vRNA segments in H3N2 viruses is largely conserved over time.
source: We further demonstrate that evolutionary relatedness between vRNA segments in H3N2 viruses is largely conserved over time.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Parallel evolution cannot be attributed solely to protein interactions.
source: Importantly, our data suggest that parallel evolution cannot be attributed solely to protein interactions, and we successfully predicted intracellular colocalization between two coevolved vRNA segments during infection with an H3N2 virus.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the Discussion.

claim: The authors successfully predicted intracellular colocalization between two coevolved vRNA segments (PB2 and NA) during infection with an H3N2 virus.
source: Importantly, our data suggest that parallel evolution cannot be attributed solely to protein interactions, and we successfully predicted intracellular colocalization between two coevolved vRNA segments during infection with an H3N2 virus.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the Discussion, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Binding of vRNA segments by NP is non-uniform and non-random.
source: We previously demonstrated that binding of vRNA segments by NP is non-uniform and non-random (Le Sage et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2017), supporting the model that intersegmental RNA interactions facilitate selective assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with supporting citations.

claim: The interaction network between vRNA segments is highly flexible and varies between H1N1 and H3N2 viruses.
source: Biochemical approaches to define bona fide intersegmental RNA-RNA interactions demonstrated that the interaction network is highly flexible and varies between H1N1 and H3N2 viruses (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Relationships between PB1, PA, NP, and NA are enriched over other segments in H3N2 viruses and conserved over time.
source: For example, we found that relationships between PB1, PA, NP, and NA are enriched over other segments in H3N2 viruses and conserved over time.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion.

claim: The polymerase subunits PB2, PB1, and PA form a supramolecular complex around each vRNA segment with NP.
source: One might expect PB1, PA, and NP to coevolve because of the functions of the proteins they encode: the polymerase subunits PB2, PB1, and PA form a supramolecular complex around each vRNA segment with NP (Fodor, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Parallel evolution of NA with PB1, PA, and NP could be driven by RNA-RNA interactions.
source: However, this explanation does not account for the parallel evolution observed between vRNP components and NA, and our microscopy data demonstrates that the NA segment preferentially colocalizes with the vRNA of one such vRNP component, supporting the possibility that parallel evolution of NA with PB1, PA, and NP could also be driven by RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the tree similarity and microscopy data.

claim: RNA relationships with the NA segment may facilitate selective assembly of vRNA segments.
source: These observations suggest that RNA relationships with the NA segment may facilitate selective assembly of vRNA segments.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: Previous pandemic influenza viruses emerged through reassortment.
source: Previous pandemic influenza viruses emerged through reassortment (Neumann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with a supporting citation.

claim: The vRNA interactome is distinct among virus strains and highly plastic.
source: As we have discussed, experimental investigations of intersegmental RNA interactions indicate that the vRNA interactome is distinct among virus strains and highly plastic (Dadonaite et al., 2019; Le Sage et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Investigation of epistatic relationships between vRNA segments through phylogenetics could inform sequence-based implementation of barriers to reassortment in emerging influenza viruses.
source: Thus, investigation of epistatic relationships between vRNA segments through phylogenetics could inform sequence-based implementation of barriers to reassortment in emerging influenza viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the approach.

claim: A549 cells were infected with A/Perth/16/2009 (H3N2) at a multiplicity of infection of 2.
source: A549 cells were infected with A/Perth/16/2009 (H3N2) at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 2 or mock-infected.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 7 legend as an experimental method.

claim: Cells were fixed at 8 hr post-infection for FISH-IF analysis.
source: Cells were fixed at 8 hr post-infection and combination fluorescence in situ hybridization/immunofluorescence (FISH and IF, respectively) was performed.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 7 legend as an experimental method.

claim: A cutoff of 97% sequence identity was selected for clustering based on the observation that it produced vRNA trees with an intermediate number of clusters.
source: We selected a cutoff of 97% sequence identity based on the observation that it produced vRNA trees with an intermediate number of clusters (16–17 clusters in each species tree).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological decision in the Results.

claim: More than half of all branches were consistently supported in PB2, PB1, and HA trees.
source: Using this approach, more than half of all branches were consistently supported in PB2, PB1, and HA trees; however, NS trees remained largely unsupported regardless of the sequence identity cutoff selected.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: NS trees remained largely unsupported regardless of the sequence identity cutoff selected.
source: Using this approach, more than half of all branches were consistently supported in PB2, PB1, and HA trees; however, NS trees remained largely unsupported regardless of the sequence identity cutoff selected.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The 95% confidence interval for RF corresponding to trees with 12 leaves was 15.3.
source: Low tree distances rarely occurred by chance, with the vast majority of tree distances being greater than 15 in null trees.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The 95% confidence interval for RF corresponding to trees with 9 leaves was 8.6.
source: The 95% confidence interval cutoff for RF corresponding to trees with nine leaves was 8.6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) and is the threshold used for statistical comparison of parallel evolution in vRNA segments from pre-pandemic and post-pandemic H1N1 strains.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.
